title: In Defence of Boredom
subtitle: Ensayo: ¿y si aburrirse fuera bueno para nosotros?

paragraphs: When was the last time you were genuinely bored? Not mildly impatient in a queue, or restless during a meeting that should have been an email, but properly, deeply bored, with nothing to do and nothing to look at, for long enough that the feeling began to change into something else? If you are like most people I know, the honest answer is that you can't remember. The moment boredom threatens, we reach for our phones. A few seconds of waiting for a kettle to boil, and the screen is already glowing in our hands. What we have quietly abolished, without ever deciding to, is one of the oldest experiences of human life.

It is tempting to see this as an unambiguous triumph. Boredom, after all, has a terrible reputation. It is associated with wasted time, wasted youth and, in its more extreme forms, with restlessness, overeating and risky behaviour. Generations of children have been told that only boring people get bored, a phrase which, on reflection, manages to be both unkind and logically questionable. If technology has finally freed us from this unpleasant state, surely we should be grateful. And yet a growing number of psychologists, philosophers and, interestingly, designers are beginning to suspect that we may have lost something valuable along the way.

It is worth remembering, too, that boredom as we understand it is a surprisingly recent idea. The English word itself only became common in the nineteenth century, and one of its earliest well-known appearances is in a novel by Charles Dickens, published in the 1850s, where a wealthy, listless character is described as suffering from it. That is not to say that earlier generations never felt restless or weary; they clearly did, and they had words for it. But the notion that ordinary people might have spare time and not know what to do with it is, historically speaking, something of a luxury. Boredom, in this sense, is a problem that only becomes possible once survival is no longer a full-time occupation.

Consider, first, how uncomfortable most of us have become with our own company. In a well-known series of experiments carried out in the United States in 2014, volunteers were asked to sit alone in a plain room for between six and fifteen minutes, with no phone, no book and nothing to do but think. Most of them reported that they did not enjoy it. More strikingly, in one version of the study, participants were given the option of pressing a button that delivered a mild but unpleasant electric shock. A majority of the men and around a quarter of the women chose to shock themselves at least once rather than simply sit with their thoughts. Whatever else this tells us, it suggests that doing nothing is far harder than it sounds.

Why should this matter? Part of the answer lies in what the mind does when it is not being given instructions. Far from switching off, the brain at rest becomes surprisingly active, wandering between memories, plans and half-formed ideas. It is in this unfocused state, researchers argue, that many of our most original connections are made. The cliché of the scientist who solves a problem in the shower, or the writer who finds the ending of a novel while staring out of a train window, exists for a reason. Rarely does inspiration arrive while we are busily answering emails.

There is some evidence to support this, although it should be treated with appropriate caution. In one study conducted in Britain, participants were first asked to complete a deliberately tedious task, copying numbers out of a telephone directory, before being asked to think of as many uses as possible for a pair of plastic cups. Those who had been bored first came up with more ideas, and more imaginative ones, than those who had gone straight to the creative task. The effect was modest, the sample was small, and it would be unwise to build a philosophy of life on a single experiment involving plastic cups. Nevertheless, the finding fits neatly with what many artists have long claimed about their own work.

What boredom seems to provide, in other words, is not ideas themselves but the conditions in which ideas can grow. It acts as a kind of signal, an uncomfortable push telling us that our current situation is not satisfying and that we should look for something better. Seen in this light, the feeling is not a defect to be eliminated but a useful, if unpleasant, piece of information. The problem with instant distraction is that it silences the signal before we have had a chance to listen to it. We resolve the discomfort, but we also lose the push.

Philosophers, as one might expect, have been arguing about the subject for considerably longer than psychologists. Some have treated boredom as something close to a moral danger; the Danish thinker Søren Kierkegaard famously described it as the root of all evil. Others have been more forgiving. In the 1930s the British philosopher Bertrand Russell devoted a chapter of a book on happiness to the question, arguing that a certain capacity to endure boredom was essential to a happy life, and that a generation unable to tolerate it would be a generation of small, restless people, cut off from the slow processes of nature. Whether or not one accepts his conclusion, it is striking how modern the warning sounds, written decades before the first television entered most homes.

I first started thinking seriously about this during a long train journey a few years ago. My phone battery had died somewhere outside Birmingham, and having finished my book, I found myself facing three hours with nothing to do. For the first half hour I was irritable, almost anxious, checking my dead phone out of habit as if it might have come back to life. Then, gradually, something shifted. I began to notice the landscape, the conversations around me, the odd shape of a cloud. By the time the train pulled into the station, I had planned an article, solved a problem that had been troubling me at work for weeks and, rather embarrassingly, written a short poem on the back of a ticket. I would not claim it was a good poem. But I had not written one in twenty years.

It would be easy, at this point, to slip into nostalgia, and I want to resist that temptation. Previous generations were not wiser simply because they had fewer devices. Plenty of people in the past experienced boredom not as a creative opportunity but as a grinding, exhausting condition, particularly those trapped in repetitive work with no prospect of escape. Nobody who has spent years on a factory production line is likely to romanticise tedium. The question is not whether boredom is good in itself, which it clearly is not, but whether brief, chosen periods of it might be worth protecting in a culture that has made them almost impossible.

There is also a danger of turning the defence of boredom into yet another self-improvement project, something to be scheduled, optimised and measured. One can already imagine the apps: ten minutes of guided boredom, with a progress bar and a weekly report. The irony would be complete. The value of an empty half hour lies precisely in the fact that it is not supposed to produce anything. The moment we begin to treat it as a tool for productivity, we have arguably missed the point altogether.

It may also help to distinguish boredom from two states with which it is often confused. Rest is chosen and restorative: an afternoon in the garden, a long bath, a walk with no particular destination. Exhaustion is the opposite, a depletion so complete that the mind has nothing left to wander with. Boredom sits somewhere between the two. It is the restlessness of a mind that still has energy but has not yet found a use for it, which is precisely why it can be so productive, and so unbearable, at the same time.

So what might a more balanced relationship with boredom look like in practice? The suggestions offered by researchers are, perhaps disappointingly, rather modest. Leave your phone in your pocket while you wait for the bus. Walk somewhere without headphones once in a while. Allow children a certain amount of unstructured time, even if they complain about it loudly, as they almost certainly will. None of these is revolutionary. What they share is a willingness to tolerate a little discomfort, for a little while, on the assumption that something interesting may be waiting on the other side of it.

For parents, in particular, this can be surprisingly difficult. It is natural to want to rescue a bored child, to offer a screen or an activity the moment the complaints begin. Yet many teachers and child psychologists argue that learning to cope with boredom is itself an important skill, one that underpins concentration, patience and the ability to entertain oneself. A child who is never allowed to be bored may never discover that boredom passes, or that the most absorbing games are often the ones invented out of nothing on a rainy afternoon.

Employers, too, might have something to learn. Many workplaces are designed to keep people constantly occupied, as if any moment of apparent idleness were a cost to be reduced. Open-plan offices, endless notifications and back-to-back meetings leave little room for the kind of unfocused thinking from which new ideas tend to emerge. Some companies have experimented with protected time in which employees are free to think, read or simply stare out of the window without having to justify it. Whether such schemes genuinely encourage creativity or merely look good in recruitment brochures is, admittedly, difficult to establish. But the instinct behind them seems sound.

None of this is to suggest that technology is the enemy. The same devices that rescue us from every idle moment also connect us with friends, give us access to more knowledge than any previous generation could have imagined and, on occasion, provide exactly the distraction we need on a bad day. The point is not to reject them but to notice what we give up each time we reach for them automatically. A tool we use deliberately is a very different thing from a habit that uses us.

Designers, whose job it often is to capture and hold our attention, have begun to ask some uncomfortable questions of their own. Many of the products we use every day are deliberately built so that there is never a natural point at which to stop: the next video starts automatically, the feed never reaches an end, and every pause is filled before we have noticed it. A small but growing number of designers argue that this is not inevitable, and that technology could be built to respect empty moments rather than eliminate them, for instance by introducing deliberate pauses, or by making it slightly harder to keep scrolling late at night. Whether companies whose income depends on our attention will ever adopt such ideas voluntarily is, to put it mildly, open to question.

There is something faintly comic about writing two thousand words in praise of doing nothing, and I am aware of the contradiction. Had I been properly bored while writing this essay, it might have been shorter and considerably better. But the argument, I think, stands. Boredom is uncomfortable because it is a question: is this really how you want to spend your time? We have become extraordinarily skilled at avoiding that question. What we have not yet learned is how to sit with it long enough to hear what our own minds have to say in reply.

So the next time you find yourself in a queue, or on a delayed train, or waiting for the kettle to boil, you might try an experiment of your own. Leave the phone where it is. Notice the restlessness, the small internal voice that insists you are wasting time. Let it complain for a while. And then see what happens next. You may well find nothing at all. Or you may find, as I did somewhere outside Birmingham, that the mind left to its own devices has a few surprises waiting.

questions.question: What does the writer suggest in the first paragraph?
options: We have stopped experiencing real boredom without consciously choosing to.
Most people are bored more often than before.
Phones have made waiting more boring.

questions.question: How does the writer regard the phrase "only boring people get bored"?
options: As wise advice for children.
As unkind and not very logical.
As scientifically proven.

questions.question: What does the 2014 experiment described in paragraph 3 suggest?
options: Electric shocks make people more creative.
Women are more easily bored than men.
Many people find being alone with their thoughts very difficult.

questions.question: How does the writer present the British study with the plastic cups?
options: As interesting but limited evidence.
As final proof that boredom causes creativity.
As a badly designed experiment that should be ignored.

questions.question: According to paragraph 6, what is the problem with instant distraction?
options: It makes boredom last longer.
It removes the signal that could push us towards something better.
It is more unpleasant than boredom.

questions.question: Why does the writer mention the poem written on the train?
options: To prove he is a talented poet.
To complain about rail travel.
To show that boredom unexpectedly led to creative activity.

questions.question: In paragraph 8, what is the writer careful to avoid?
options: Pretending that boredom in the past was always positive.
Criticising factory work.
Talking about previous generations.

questions.question: What does "A tool we use deliberately is a very different thing from a habit that uses us" mean?
options: Habits are more useful than tools.
Technology is fine when we choose to use it, not when we use it automatically.
We should stop using technology completely.

questions.question: What is the tone of the final paragraph?
options: Strongly critical of the reader.
Pessimistic about the future.
Gently persuasive: it invites the reader to try something.

exam_practice.title: Uso del inglés · Una palabra por hueco
exam_practice.instructions: Como en los exámenes oficiales: escribe una sola palabra en cada hueco.

items.text: ___ we have quietly abolished is one of the oldest experiences of human life. It is in this unfocused state ___ many original connections are made. Rarely ___ inspiration arrive while we are answering emails.
items.hint: Pseudo-cleft: What … is. Inversión tras Rarely: does + sujeto + verbo.

items.text: Volunteers ___ asked to sit alone in a plain room. Participants were given the option ___ pressing a button. ___ finished my book, I found myself with nothing to do.
items.hint: The option of + -ing. Having + participio para la acción previa.

items.text: By the time the train pulled ___ the station, I ___ planned an article. The effect was modest; ___, the finding fits with what artists have claimed.
items.hint: Past perfect para lo que ya había ocurrido antes de otro momento pasado.

exam_practice.title: Formación de palabras
exam_practice.instructions: Escribe una palabra derivada de la que está entre paréntesis (por ejemplo, DECIDE → decision).

items.text: Boredom is not a defect to be ___ (ELIMINATE) quickly. Learning to cope with it requires a ___ (WILLING) to tolerate discomfort. Workplaces see any moment of ___ (IDLE) as a cost.
The study was ___ (DELIBERATE) tedious. ___ (ADMIT), it is hard to know whether such schemes work. The writer is ___ (EXTRAORDINARY) skilled at avoiding the question, he says.
items.hint: Adverbios en -ly; admittedly reconoce algo antes de matizar.

items.text: Most people found the experience ___ (PLEASANT). Children need time that is ___ (STRUCTURE). The writer resists the temptation of ___ (NOSTALGIC).
items.hint: Prefijo negativo un-; nombre a partir del adjetivo.

exam_practice.title: Transformaciones
exam_practice.instructions: Completa la segunda frase para que signifique lo mismo que la primera. Usa la palabra entre paréntesis sin cambiarla y entre dos y cinco palabras.

items.text: "I would have written a shorter essay if I had been properly bored." → Had ___ (BORED), this essay might have been shorter.
items.explanation: Inversión en el tercer condicional: Had + sujeto + participio = If + sujeto + had + participio.

items.text: "It is quite likely that you will find nothing at all." → You ___ (WELL) nothing at all.
"People started to suspect that something valuable had been lost." → It ___ (SUSPECTED) that something valuable had been lost.
"I didn't know then that I would write a poem that day." → Little ___ (KNOW) I was going to write a poem that day.
"Children will almost certainly complain loudly." → Children are ___ (BOUND) loudly.
"Boredom is not good in itself, but brief periods of it might be valuable." → While boredom ___ (ITSELF), brief periods of it might be valuable.
answers: is not good in and of itself
